title: Removing shell=True from subprocess calls
summary: See rule DPK-SAST-003 fire on a synthetic file, switch to an argument list with shell=False, and verify the finding is gone on rescan.
concept: subprocess with shell=True passes the command through a system shell. Shell metacharacters — spaces, quotes, semicolons, backticks — in attacker-influenced input then become OS command injection. The safe pattern is an argument list with no shell: the operating system receives each argument exactly, with no parsing step where input can escape into syntax. This lesson pairs with pack rule DPK-SAST-003, which flags the lexical shape shell=True on one line. The rule is line-based and conservative: it cannot prove taint, so every hit is review-required rather than proven exploitable.
objectives: Explain why shell=True turns input into shell syntax.
Recognise the shell=True flag in review and in scan findings.
Convert a shell command to an argument list and verify by rescan.

practice.instruction: Import the starter file into one of your OWN projects, run a SAST scan, and find rule DPK-SAST-003. Read the finding, then apply the fix (argument list with shell=False from the fixed file), upload the fixed file, and run SAST again to verify the finding is no longer observed.
practice.fixInstruction: Replace the shell string with an argument list and shell=False, so each argument is passed exactly with no shell parsing step.

quiz.prompt: What does shell=True change about a subprocess call?
options: The command passes through a system shell that parses metacharacters
The command can only run git
quiz.explanation: The shell parsing step is where input escapes into syntax. An argument list with shell=False has no such step.

quiz.prompt: Which fix removes the injection channel?
options: Logging the command before running it
quiz.explanation: argv passes each argument exactly. Lowercasing and logging leave the shell parsing step intact.
